title: Mismatch Metrics Runbook — stream stalls & burst 429s
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working runbook for oncall responders and engineers who encounter the following correlated API symptoms: increased client-visible timeouts, sudden bursts of 429 rate-limited responses, degraded or truncated streaming payloads, and elevated internal error rates. It focuses on detection heuristics, immediate mitigation recipes, quick validation checks, and guidance for post-incident synthesis.

Design origin / motivation:
We often see incidents where surface-level alerts (latency spike or 429s) don't match internal capacity signals. The root cause in several past events was a metric divergence — client-side request rates or payload sizes change faster than routing/policy engines adapt, which then triggers throttles or causes backend workers to stall while attempting large KV/cache loads. To reduce pager noise and speed recovery, this doc codifies a few pragmatic heuristics and short mitigations we can apply during the first 30–90 minutes of an event.

Definitions / key signals to watch:
- Client latency p50/p95/p99 (edge).
- Server processing latency (per model group / pool).
- 429 rate (per route / model).
- Stream abort rate (percent of streams terminated early by runtime).
- Downstream queue length (async task queue backlog).
- Metric Divergence Index (MDI): a simple ratio we use for quick triage: client_incoming_qps / observed_serving_capacity_qps (smoothed 1m). MDI > 1.5 for > 2m is a fast indicator of a mismatch.

Detection: quick alert correlation (first 5 minutes)
1) Alert inbox: if we get any of these alerts within a short window, treat as one incident: latency p95 > 500ms; 429 rate > 3% of requests in 1m; stream-abort-rate > 1%; internal error-rate spike > 2x baseline.
2) Run the MDI check: query Prometheus or Metrics service for client_incoming_qps and sum of pool capacity qps (consider currently active workers). If MDI > 1.5, proceed to mismatch mitigations.
3) Confirm traffic shift: check CDN/ingress logs for sudden client IP concentration, large request payload growth (longer prompt tokens), or spike in streaming connections from a single customer or region.

Quick mitigation (first 10 minutes): low-risk actions you can safely attempt from pager
- Toggle routing to lighter-configured pools (if available) for affected routes: switch to model-variant with shorter max-seq or lower batch-size. This reduces per-request processing time.
  - How: use control-plane CLI: redwood route update --route <route> --fallback-variant <small-variant>
  - When to revert: when p95 latency and 429% return to baseline for 10m.
- Reduce per-request token limits at edge for suspect customer(s): set throttle max_tokens= from 4096 -> 1024 (edge-layer policy).
- Enable short-lived adaptive throttling: flip edge policy from permissive to conservative for route (adjust weight to 0.5). This reduces client concurrency quickly while keeping service online.
- Temporarily reduce streaming window size on server-side (cut chunk size) to avoid long-running KV cache loads.
- If 429s are region-specific, failover traffic to other regions with capacity (smart routing).

Medium-risk mitigations (10–30 minutes): require coordination with owner or SRE lead
- Scale up serving pool capacity (add nodes) if autoscaling is slow/disabled. Note: prefer horizontal add to avoid slow warm-up of large GPU kernels.
- Enable or increase prefix/KV caching for common prompt patterns (requires config push).
- Apply temporary rate-limits to heavy API keys (identified by API key or customer header) — target known high-traffic customers first. Be careful with customer SLA.
- Disable non-essential instrumentation that increases CPU/IO on worker side (debug logging, trace sampling).

Fast triage checklist (commands & queries)
- PromQL to estimate MDI (example):
  client_in_qps = sum(rate(edge_requests_total{route=~"<route>"}[1m]))
  serve_capacity_qps = sum(nodes_capacity_qps{pool=~"<pool>"})
  MDI = client_in_qps / max(serve_capacity_qps, 1)
- Check error distribution: group by model variant and route: rate(backend_errors_total[5m]) by (model_variant, route)
- Stream aborts: sum(rate(stream_abort_total[1m])) by (route, region)
- Ingress logs sample: tail last 500 entries for route: gsutil or bigquery query or direct log tail. Look for sudden increases in token_count or connection churn.
- Check worker health pages: queue depth, CPU, GPU mem, swap, stuck threads (runtime /proc traces), and last GC pause.

Immediate validation steps after mitigation (first 5–10 minutes after action)
- Confirm p95 latency falls or 429% drops by at least 30% relative to peak.
- Confirm error-rate trend slopes downward for 3 consecutive 1m buckets.
- Validate no new customer-facing degradations introduced (sample deterministic synthetic requests).

Communication templates (Slack + incident bridge)
- Short Slack post to #sre-oncall: "INCIDENT: high 429s & stream stalls on /v1/chat for region-us-east. MDI=1.9. Flipped route fallback-variant -> small-quantized. Observing p95 down ~35% — continuing to monitor. TAG: @oncall. SRE ticket: SRE-XXXX."
- Customer-facing status blurb (for CS): "We are experiencing elevated request throttles in US-East affecting streaming sessions. We have activated conservative routing and rate-limits for heavy sessions; teams are actively scaling capacity. ETA to stable: 30–45m. Updates will be posted to status.redwood.com and here."

When to escalate to engineers or exec oncall
- Rolling customer errors (more than 5 customers cross-application) and recovery mitigation does not improve key metrics after 15 minutes.
- Evidence of data-plane corruption (e.g., persistent model errors, corrupted responses).
- Autoscaler not responding or health pages show many provisioning failures.

Root-cause investigation starters (post-first-response)
- Correlate ingress patterns with customer deployments / releases: check recent deploys (last 30m) via GitHub PRs and console rollouts.
- Look for policy/regression: did the rate-limiter/policy config change? (Console change logs).
- Examine model-controller logs for kernel selection failures or OOMs during batch formation. Batching pathological cases often manifest as stalls rather than immediate OOMs.
- Check cache hit-rate for KV/prefix caches: sudden drop in cache hit-rate can cause much larger per-request work.

Recovery and rollback guidance
- If a configuration change caused the incident (policy or routing), roll back that change, revert to last-known-good for that route, and monitor for 10–15 minutes.
- If scaling is required, prefer rolling addition of small nodes (avoid single huge node) to keep warm-up short.
- When using fallback variants, include a follow-up plan to re-evaluate quality regressions (A/B sample) and lift fallbacks only after 1h stable.

Post-incident synthesis checklist (owner responsibilities)
- Create an incident timeline with events (alerts, mitigation actions, who did what) and publish to SRE ticket.
- Compute MDI time-series and confirm hypothesis. Include evidence of cache/misroute/traffic-change.
- Add targeted alerting: create an MDI-based alert that fires earlier (e.g., MDI > 1.2 sustained 3m) so we can detect divergence before client-visible saturations.
- TODOs: automated small-variant fallback experiment (A/B) to validate tradeoffs, tune autoscaler thresholds to act earlier on sustained token-rate increases, add per-customer token-length rate metrics to alert.

Notes and heuristics from prior incidents (lessons learned)
- Conservative throttles at the edge are less painful than bulk throttling inside the runtime — failing earlier keeps the runtime healthy.
- Large, low-entropy prompts can occupy KV cache and cause downstream stalls; short-circuiting those at the edge is effective.
- Streaming chunk size matters: tiny more-frequent chunks reduce per-chunk latency but increase connection pressure; tune based on observed connection churn.

Appendix: quick commands (examples)
- Switch route variant: redwood route update --route /v1/chat --fallback-variant small-quantized-2 --reason "oncall mitigation - reduce processing time"
- Add temporary customer rate-limit: redwood rate-limits add --api-key <key> --qps 5 --burst 10 --ttl 30m
- Sample PromQL for stream abort rate: sum(rate(stream_abort_total{route="/v1/chat"}[1m])) by (region)

Open questions and follow-ups (to be assigned)
- Should we add per-token-rate autoscaler that considers token-size instead of just request QPS? (assigned: Marco Li)
- Experiment: can we pre-warm a small pool of quantized variants in each region to avoid cold-start stalls? (assigned: Tanya)

End of draft — please add short reproductions, failed playbook runs, or links to incident pages below when updating this doc.
